item.title: Rethinking mitochondrial aging: what 750,000 genomes tell us about longevity
item.description: Gupta et al. (Nature 2026) analyzed 736,000 whole-genome sequences and upended the oxidative-damage theory of mitochondrial aging. Blood mtSNV mutations look like replication errors amplified by clonal hematopoiesis, not wear-and-tear.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, mitochondrial aging was explained as oxidative rust. A new Nature study of 736,000 people says blood mtDNA mutations look like replication copy-errors amplified by clonal hematopoiesis in bone marrow, not daily wear-and-tear.

What changed: mutations spike around age 60 because hidden stem-cell clones expand, not because cells suddenly start rusting. That reframes antioxidants, mitophagy, and what to track next.
